a female given name from Old Norse [in turn from Ancient Greek], equivalent to English Karina

1001049.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Kaðrina (“female given name”), a later form of Katrina (“female given name”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη (Aikaterínē, “female given name”). In Old Norse, the consonant sequence in Katrina developed from tr to ðr, after which ð was lost, yielding Karina. The original meaning is uncertain, though the name was associated early with καθαρός (katharós, “pure, chaste”). First attested in the 15th century in Norway.
Compare Danish Karina, Swedish Karina and Faroese Karina (“female given name”).

en.g: Used with adjectives, and occasionally verbal stems, to form inchoative or fientive verbs meaning “to become, turn, or grow ...”

1001305.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse -na (“used to form inchoative verbs”), from Proto-Germanic *-inōną, a verb-forming suffix used to form inchoative verbs. Also partly merged with or influenced by Proto-Germanic *-naną (“to become the base”), another Germanic fientive verb-forming suffix in *-n-.
The modern Bokmål form reflects the regular infinitive ending -e, replacing Old Norse infinitive -a.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -ne and -na, Icelandic -na, Faroese -na Swedish -na, Danish -ne, English -en and Scots -en.

en.g: a waning moon; the Moon while it is in a waning phase
x: paa den blaableke himmel svævet et hvitt fnug av maanenæ
against the pale-blue sky floated a white wisp of the waning Moon

1002073.etyen:
From måne (“moon”) + ne (“waning phase of the Moon”), literally “moon waning”. The second element ne denotes the period in which the Moon is waning, between full moon and new moon, and continues Old Norse nið or niðar, with the basic meaning “decline, waning”. The deeper origin of the Old Norse word is uncertain; it may be related to niðr (“down”).
Compare the parallel Danish formation Danish Maanenæ (“waning moon”). The Norwegian word is attested in the older spelling maanenæ in Sigrid Undset's Vaaren (1914); the available sources do not establish whether the Norwegian formation arose indepen

1004889.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἐγκέλαδος (Enkélados, “Enkelados, a Giant in Greek mythology”). The Ancient Greek name has long been associated with κέλαδος (kélados, “noise, din, clamour”), and has traditionally been interpreted as referring to a noisy or resounding figure, perhaps with ἐν (en, “in, within”) as its first element. The exact prehistoric formation of the name is not entirely certain.
The astronomical name Enceladus is the Latinized form of the same mythological name, through Latin Enceladus (“Enkelados”), and was given to a moon of Saturn in honour of the Giant.
